title: Letters, the IPA and phonetic features

blocks.main: **Letters are not phonemes, so researchers need one standard system for writing the sounds of every language.** Each writing system has its own spelling conventions. Pinyin is perfectly regular for Mandarin, and French spelling is also very regular. An English reader still mispronounces “Wo qu tushuguan” or “Comment tu t’appelles?” because English letter habits do not carry over.
sub: The **International Phonetic Alphabet** (IPA) gives one symbol per speech sound, so sounds can be compared directly across languages.
Its consonant chart is a system of comparisons, because a symbol’s position tells you how the sound is made.
blocks.end: So the IPA lets speech scientists talk precisely about how sounds in different languages are similar and different.

blocks.main: **The consonant chart is organized by three features, place, manner and voicing.** **Place of articulation** (where the vocal tract closes or narrows) runs along the top from the front of the mouth to the back. **Manner of articulation** (how closed the passage is) runs down the side from fully closed to open. **Voicing** (when the vocal folds start vibrating relative to the closure) separates the members of each pair.
sub: /p/ is a plosive, bilabial and not voiced. /b/ is a plosive, bilabial and voiced.
So /p/ and /b/ share manner and place and differ only in the timing of phonation relative to the release of the closure.
The same voicing difference separates /t/ from /d/, so we can talk in general about “the voiced stops” /b/, /d/ and /g/.
The features are anchored to real movements of the vocal tract. Examples are both lips closing, the lower lip meeting the upper teeth, or air flowing through the nose.
blocks.end: So features let two sounds be described precisely as sharing two properties and differing in a third.

blocks.main: **The same voicing contrast is produced differently across languages and contexts.** In English, the first sound of “peer” is often an unvoiced **aspirated** stop [pʰ], with a puff of air after the release. The first sound of “beer” is often an unvoiced, unaspirated stop [p]. In most varieties of French, the contrast is really between [p] in “pou” and [b] in “boue.”
sub: Putting a hand in front of the mouth while saying peer and beer lets you feel the aspiration.
**Slashes** mark **broad transcription** (writing the phonemes of an utterance), as in /p/.
**Square brackets** mark **narrow transcription** (including as much detail as possible), as in [pʰ].
blocks.end: So broad transcription records the categories that tell words apart, and narrow transcription records how each sound was actually produced.

blocks.main: **Vowels are described by tongue height, frontness and lip rounding, but real vowels are messier than one point on a chart.** Close vowels tend to have a higher jaw position than open vowels. Front vowels have the tongue body farther forward than back vowels. **Rounding** of the lips is a separate dimension.
sub: /y/ is the vowel in French “tu” and Mandarin “qu.” Making an /i/ and then rounding the lips turns it toward /y/.
Some vowels, like the **diphthongs** in “boat” and “bait,” are very dynamic, because the tongue moves during the vowel.
Vowels also differ across dialects. In the mid-Atlantic dialect of New York City’s outer boroughs, CAUGHT and COT have different vowels. Most other Americans say them the same way.
blocks.end: So a vowel chart gives useful reference points, but each speaker’s vowel system has to be checked by listening to that speaker.

questions.q: Why do we need the IPA when languages already have alphabets?
questions.a: We need the IPA because letters are not phonemes, and each writing system uses its own spelling conventions. Even regular systems like Pinyin and French spelling cannot be read correctly with English letter habits. The IPA gives one standard symbol per sound, so sounds can be compared accurately across languages.

questions.q: What three features organize the IPA consonant chart?
questions.a: The chart is organized by place, manner and voicing. Place of articulation runs from the front of the vocal tract to the back, and manner runs from fully closed to open. Voicing separates the members of each pair by when the vocal folds start vibrating relative to the closure.

questions.q: How are /p/ and /b/ alike, and how are they different?
questions.a: /p/ and /b/ are alike in manner and place, because both are bilabial plosives. They differ in voicing, which is the timing of phonation relative to the release of the closure. The same difference separates /t/ from /d/, so we can describe a whole class of voiced stops /b/, /d/ and /g/.

questions.q: What is the difference between /p/ and [pʰ]?
questions.a: /p/ is a broad transcription that names the phoneme, while [pʰ] is a narrow transcription of one specific pronunciation. Slashes mark the category a language uses to tell words apart. Square brackets record as much detail as possible, such as the aspiration in the first sound of “peer.”

questions.q: How do English and French differ in producing the voicing contrast for stops?
questions.a: English often contrasts an aspirated [pʰ] in “peer” with an unaspirated [p] in “beer,” so neither sound is fully voiced. Most varieties of French contrast [p] in “pou” with a truly voiced [b] in “boue.” So the same broad labels, voiced and voiceless, are produced in different ways in different languages.

blocks.main: **A minimal pair proves that two sounds are different phonemes in a language.** A **minimal pair** is two words whose difference in meaning depends on a difference in one sound. If two phones are **contrastive** in this way, they are examples of different phonemes. CAUGHT and COT are a minimal pair for a speaker who distinguishes the two low back vowels.
sub: Minimal pairs also reveal which feature a contrast depends on.
In English, /b/ and /p/, /t/ and /d/, and /k/ and /g/ all differ on voicing. We know this by comparing minimal pairs in English itself.
blocks.end: So the evidence for a phoneme always comes from word contrasts in the language being studied.

blocks.main: **Allophones are different phones that count as the same phoneme because no minimal pair separates them.** Phonemes are realized in many ways, and some of this variation is very predictable. Recordings of “pot that,” “spot that” and “stop that” make it possible to compare how /p/ is released and aspirated in each position.
sub: We sometimes say [stɑpʰ] with an aspirated release, often when stressing the word or speaking clearly in citation form.
There is no difference in meaning between [stɑp̚] and [stɑpʰ], and no minimal pair separates these two phones in these contexts.
So they are **allophones**, from allo meaning different, which gives “different phones for the same phoneme.”
The forms “stop,” “stops,” “stopped” and “stopping” put /p/ in new positions, so its release and aspiration change with the morphological form.
blocks.end: So hearing a difference between two sounds does not make them different phonemes, because only a meaning contrast does that.

blocks.main: **The word voicing is used in two different ways.** In narrow transcription of specific phones, a sound is called voiced if the vocal folds vibrate during the whole sound. In broad transcription of phonemes, voicing is a contrast that can be realized in several ways.
sub: One realization is the presence or absence of aspiration at the beginnings of words.
Another is the relative duration of voicing to closure, as in “writer” and “rider.”
blocks.end: So an English “voiced” stop can be a phoneme in the voiced category even when its vocal folds are not vibrating the whole time.

blocks.main: **Phonotactics are the rules for which phonemes can occur together in syllables.** English allows [spɑroʊ] or [zbɑroʊ] but never [sbɑroʊ], whatever the speaker thinks they are saying. When English speakers meet clusters their language forbids, they change them.
sub: The Polish name Zbigniew becomes [zɨ’bIg.nʲu].
The name Gbagbo becomes [gə.bɑ.gə.boʊ], with vowels inserted to break up the clusters.
blocks.end: So the sound patterns of a language shape how its speakers produce even foreign words.

blocks.main: **A phoneme is the smallest phonetic unit in a language that is capable of conveying a distinction in meaning.** Phonemes are not letters. They are not even specific sounds or gestures, because one phoneme can have several allophones.
sub: The IPA gives speech scientists a way to talk about similarities and differences between sounds across languages.
It is easy to think of the IPA as an “alphabet of phonemes,” but this is a mistake because phonemes are not letters.
blocks.end: So a phoneme is defined by the meaning contrasts it creates, not by a symbol or a single sound.

questions.q: What is a minimal pair, and what does it establish?
questions.a: A minimal pair is two words whose difference in meaning depends on a difference in a single sound. It establishes that the two sounds are contrastive, so they are different phonemes in that language. CAUGHT and COT do this for a speaker whose dialect keeps the two low back vowels apart.

questions.q: Why are [stɑp̚] and [stɑpʰ] allophones of /p/ rather than different phonemes?
questions.a: They are allophones because there is no difference in meaning between them. No minimal pair separates these two phones in these contexts in English. So they are different phones that realize the same phoneme /p/.

questions.q: How do minimal pairs show that English stop contrasts depend on voicing?
questions.a: English has minimal pairs for /b/ and /p/, /t/ and /d/, and /k/ and /g/. In each pair the place and manner stay the same and only voicing changes. So voicing is the shared feature that carries the contrast, and this is known from comparing minimal pairs in English.

questions.q: What are the two meanings of voicing?
questions.a: In narrow transcription, a phone is voiced if the vocal folds vibrate during the whole sound. In broad transcription, voicing is a phonemic contrast that can be realized in different ways. Those ways include aspiration at the beginnings of words and the duration of voicing relative to closure in “writer” and “rider.”

questions.q: What are phonotactics, and how do they show up in speech?
questions.a: Phonotactics are the patterns that say which phonemes can occur together in syllables. English never allows [sbɑroʊ], so speakers say [spɑroʊ] or [zbɑroʊ]. Faced with names like Zbigniew or Gbagbo, English speakers insert vowels to fit English syllable patterns.

title: Speech is a continuous signal, not a row of letters

blocks.main: **The lack of invariance problem is that one speech category has no single fixed acoustic form.** The same vowel sounds different across speakers and dialects. A listener still understands people who say “Aaron” and “Erin” with the same vowel.
sub: The vowel measurements for each category spread widely and overlap with neighboring categories.
So a listener cannot identify a vowel by checking for one fixed set of acoustic values.
blocks.end: So understanding speech means interpreting variable sound as stable categories, and this problem comes up again and again.

blocks.main: **Speech is a continuously changing signal, not an orderly stream of letter-like units.** Literate people easily imagine that speech is produced as separate letters. A spectrogram of “A sore back is a real pain” has no clean boundaries between the sounds.
sub: The lips, jaw and tongue move continuously during speech.
Each movement overlaps with the movements for neighboring sounds, so the acoustic signal blends them together.
blocks.end: So phonemes are useful categories, but they are not separate pieces lined up in the signal.

blocks.main: **Hockett (1955) compared speech to a row of raw eggs smashed through a wringer.** The eggs on the belt stand for the series of phonemes the speaker intends. The wringer smashes and mixes them, and that mess stands for the speech signal. An inspector studies the mess and decides which eggs went in.
sub: The inspector represents the hearer.
He does not have to put the eggs back together, which is physically impossible, but only to identify them.
blocks.end: So the listener’s job is to identify the intended phonemes from an overlapping signal, not to recover separate pieces.

blocks.main: **Some researchers have started to question whether phonemes are psychologically or linguistically real.** Phonemes are a useful way to describe contrasts. It is a separate question whether speakers actually store and recognize words in phoneme-sized units.
blocks.end: So the phoneme is a strong descriptive tool whose status in the mind is still debated.

questions.q: Why is it so important that phonemes are not letters?
questions.a: Phonemes are not letters because speech is a continuously changing signal, not an orderly stream of letter-like units. A spectrogram of “A sore back is a real pain” has no clean breaks between sounds. Neighboring sounds overlap, so each phoneme looks different depending on its context.

questions.q: What is the lack of invariance problem?
questions.a: The lack of invariance problem is that a single speech category has no fixed acoustic form. The same vowel varies across speakers and dialects, and the categories overlap. Listeners still understand speech, so they must map variable sounds onto stable categories.

questions.q: Explain Hockett’s egg analogy and what each part stands for.
questions.a: Hockett (1955) imagined raw eggs on a belt being smashed together by a wringer. The eggs stand for the intended phonemes, and the smashed mess stands for the speech signal. The inspector who identifies the eggs from the mess stands for the hearer, who only has to identify the phonemes, not rebuild them.

blocks.main: **Words are built from meaningful parts called morphemes, and “knifes” shows two kinds of morphology at once.** In a Scrabble argument, one player says the plural of knife is knives. The other answers that Tony “knifes” Bernardo in West Side Story. Both are right, because knife the noun and knife the verb are different words.
sub: **Derivational morphology** derives new words from existing parts, and **zero derivation** turns the noun knife into a verb with no added ending.
**Inflectional morphology** then adds -s, because the sentence “He knifes him” needs a third person singular verb.
Morphology itself is morph- (form) plus -ology (the study of), which gives “the study of the forms of words.”
blocks.end: So a word form can only be judged by its grammatical role in the sentence.

blocks.main: **Derivational morphology is productive, but in limited ways, so the meaning of a derived word is only partly predictable.** Even zero derivation usually works with a narrow sense of the base word. To “knife” somebody uses one particular kind of knife, not a butter knife.
sub: The suffix -hood means a state of being, as in brotherhood and sisterhood.
Knighthood is odd, because two brothers share their brotherhood but each knight has his own knighthood.
Neighborhood is a good word, but -hood does a different job in it, and we say friendship rather than friendhood for no clear reason.
Strong associates of knife become verbs with unrelated meanings, as in “dish it out,” “a forked tongue” and “table the issue.”
blocks.end: So derivation creates new words, but which words exist and what they mean is partly a matter of convention.

blocks.main: **Derivation often changes the pronunciation of the rest of the word, not only adding an ending.** Certificate /sər.ˈtI.fɨ.kɨt/ becomes certification /ˌsər.tɨ.fɨ.ˈkeI.ʃən/ and then recertification /ˈri.sər.tɨ.fɨ.ˌkeI.ʃən/. The stress moves and the vowels change as affixes are added.
sub: The noun and verb forms of record and invite differ mainly in stress.
This is one reason for “The Chaos” of English spelling. It is also why spelling closer to the spoken form would not necessarily improve readability.
blocks.end: So adding an affix can reshape the sound of the whole word.

blocks.main: **Inflectional morphology changes a word’s grammatical form in a predictable way and is required by the syntax.** English inflection marks plurals, as in knife and knives or one mouse and a lot of mice. It also marks third person singular present (she walks) and past tense (I walked, she sang). Menn notes that it would be silly to have separate dictionary entries for singular and plural nouns.
sub: The sound change can be irregular, as in mice and sang, even though the grammatical meaning stays predictable.
In the phrase “two [noun]+pl,” whatever noun goes there must be pluralized somehow.
No derivational form is required by syntax in this way, and a formula like “Once you [verb] it, you can un-[verb] it” is not syntax.
English uses little inflection compared with many languages. Others mark case on nouns, form plurals differently for small and large numbers, or conjugate verbs more elaborately.
blocks.end: So inflection keeps the same word but fits it to its grammatical job in the sentence.

blocks.main: **Derivation and inflection both build new forms from old parts, but they do different jobs.** Both create new phonological forms and change the meanings of base forms. **Derivation** creates new words and is productive only in limited ways. **Inflection** changes how words interact syntactically, is highly productive but not always regular, and is required by syntax.
blocks.end: So the test is whether the change makes a new word or fits the same word into a sentence.

questions.q: Why is “knifes” a word, even though the plural of knife is knives?
questions.a: “Knifes” is a word because it is the verb knife with third person singular -s, as in “He knifes him.” Knives is the plural of the noun knife. Zero derivation made knife into a verb, and inflection then added the ending the sentence requires.

questions.q: What is a morpheme, and how does the word morphology itself break into morphemes?
questions.a: A morpheme is a meaningful part that words are built from. Morphology is morph-, meaning form, plus -ology, meaning the study of. Together they give “the study of the forms of words.”

questions.q: In what ways is derivational morphology productive but limited?
questions.a: Derivation can make new words, but the meaning of the result is only partly predictable and affixes do not apply to every base. The suffix -hood works for brotherhood and sisterhood but does a different job in neighborhood. We say friendship instead of friendhood for no clear reason.

questions.q: How can derivation change the pronunciation of a word?
questions.a: Adding an affix can move the stress and change the vowels in the rest of the word. Certificate, certification and recertification each have a different stress pattern. Record and invite change stress between their noun and verb forms.

questions.q: What makes inflection different from derivation?
questions.a: Inflection changes how a word works in the sentence, while derivation creates a new word. Inflection is highly productive and required by syntax, as when “two” forces the next noun to be plural. Derivation is productive only in limited ways, and no sentence ever requires a particular derived form.

blocks.main: **A noun phrase has an abstract structure that very different word strings can share.** Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs are **content words**. **Function words** like determiners and prepositions organize them into phrases. “The video for ‘More than Words’” is a noun phrase with the structure Det. + N + PP.
sub: The is a determiner that begins the noun phrase.
For is a preposition that begins a prepositional phrase, and that phrase specifies which video is meant.
“Two guys from the early ‘nineties” and “a band with only one hit” share the Det. + N + PP structure.
blocks.end: So phrase structure describes relations among categories, not particular words.

blocks.main: **Abstract categories make it possible to compare languages that build phrases differently.** All languages have noun phrases, but they form them very differently. The Chinese phrase 咖啡店裡面的小貓 goes PP + N, with “coffeeshop inside” before “cat.”
sub: The Chinese noun phrase has no determiner.
This helps explain why determiners are so difficult for speakers of Chinese languages to learn in a second language.
blocks.end: So without abstraction we could not talk about very different surface forms as similar.

blocks.main: **Prepositional phrases are P + NP, and phrases sit inside other phrases.** “From the early ‘nineties” is a preposition followed by a noun phrase. That noun phrase has its own structure, Det + Adj. + N.
sub: The determiner, adjective and noun are inside the noun phrase.
The noun phrase is inside the prepositional phrase, which will be inside a sentence or another noun phrase.
This nesting is why people started using trees to diagram sentences.
blocks.end: So sentence structure is hierarchical, not just a string of words in a row.

blocks.main: **A clause is a verb phrase and its subject, and the subject is the noun phrase that controls the verb.** Verb phrases contain different complements, such as V + NP in “sang the song.” Another is V + NP + PP in “threw a party for him.” In the example sentence, the whole first noun phrase is the subject and its head noun is “video.”
sub: In “The plums that were in the icebox were delicious,” the verb agrees with “plums,” not “icebox.” This is because plums is the head of the noun phrase.
Adding “which you were probably saving for breakfast” puts a clause inside a clause.
Changing “you” to “my roommate” changes only the inner verb, which becomes “was saving.”
blocks.end: So agreement reveals which noun phrase controls which verb.

blocks.main: **Syntactic roles and semantic roles are different, so the subject is not always the agent.** “I have eaten the plums in the icebox” and “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me” mean the same thing. In the passive sentence, the plums are the subject, because the verb “were eaten” agrees with the plural noun.
sub: “By me” is just a prepositional phrase fleshing out the verb phrase.
**Semantic roles** describe who did what to whom, and here they are Undergoer (the plums), Location (the icebox) and **Agent** (me).
These semantic roles stay the same in both sentences.
blocks.end: So “me” feels like the subject only because English usually puts the agent in the subject position.

blocks.main: **Language is highly generative, and we do most of it without thinking.** We make new words with derivational morphology. We organize words into phrases, clauses and sentences with syntax. We modify words for their syntactic roles with inflectional morphology.
blocks.end: So some of the most complex things linguistics must explain are hiding in plain sight.

questions.q: What is the structure of “The video for ‘More than Words,’” and what job do its function words do?
questions.a: It is a noun phrase with the structure Det. + N + PP. The determiner “the” begins the noun phrase, and the preposition “for” begins a prepositional phrase that tells which video is meant. The same structure fits phrases with completely different words, such as “a band with only one hit.”

questions.q: In “The plums that were in the icebox were delicious,” why is the verb “were” and not “was”?
questions.a: The verb is “were” because it agrees with “plums,” the head of the subject noun phrase. “Icebox” is singular, but it sits inside a modifying phrase and does not control the verb. So agreement follows the head of the subject, not the nearest noun.

questions.q: In “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me,” why is “me” not the subject?
questions.a: “Me” is not the subject because the verb “were eaten” agrees with the plural noun plums, which makes the plums the subject. “By me” is a prepositional phrase inside the verb phrase. “Me” is still the agent, because semantic roles do not change between active and passive sentences.

questions.q: Why do we need abstract categories like NP to compare languages?
questions.a: We need them because languages build the same kind of phrase in very different ways. English says “the cat in the coffee shop,” while Chinese puts the location before the noun and has no determiner. Only an abstract category like NP lets us call both noun phrases and describe how they differ.

blocks.main: **Association norms record the first words people write down when they see a cue word.** Participants saw cues such as LION, TRIPE, FREE, STRIPES, PEAR, BEAR, TREE and TIGER for a few seconds. Three items, LION, TIGER and STRIPES, matter later.
sub: Pairs like TRIPE and STRIPES, or PEAR and BEAR, look alike but mean unrelated things, so the relation between form and meaning is arbitrary.
Associated is different from similar, because TIGER and STRIPES are associated even though a tiger and a stripe are not similar things.
The list itself can shape the answers, so a list of only wild animals or only household appliances could produce different associates.
blocks.end: So association norms measure which words bring each other to mind under particular task conditions.

blocks.main: **Psycholinguistics borrows its basic ideas from neuroscience, starting with activation.** These ideas are activation, spreading of activation over weighted connections, distributed representations, associative learning, and top-down and bottom-up processing. They are the basis for most theory and experimental design in the field.
sub: **Hubel and Weisel (1968)** recorded simple cells in primary visual cortex (V1) that respond to lines of particular orientations in a particular receptive field.
One cell activates most strongly to upward movement of a line at about 315°, so it represents that combination of features.
A cell further up the visual processing stream responds to something more complex, like the profile of another monkey.
blocks.end: So “activation” in psycholinguistics extends this idea, as a metaphor, to perceptual and conceptual representations.

blocks.main: **A word can be modeled as a node whose activation rises with the strength of the evidence for it.** Imagine a simple network with nodes for LION, TIGER and STRIPES. Each node can be activated by its word, in any case, font or size, so recognition faces the same lack of invariance problem as phonemes.
sub: Activation can be partial, so when LION contrasts poorly with a noise mask, its node is only weakly activated.
As the stimulus becomes clearer, activation increases.
The **signal-to-noise ratio** is how strong the word is compared with the background noise. When it is very favorable, activity is strong enough that the network has identified “lion.”
This is the **perceptual identification task**, where participants push a button as soon as they can identify the item.
blocks.end: So identification time measures how quickly a word’s activation reaches the point of recognition.

blocks.main: **How quickly a word is identified depends on the stimulus itself and on the experimental environment.** Features of the stimulus include how frequently the word is encountered and how similar it is to other words. Features of the environment include whether you just saw the same word and whether you just saw a related word.
sub: Seeing the same word again speeds identification, and this is **repetition priming**.
Seeing a similar or related word first can also change identification speed.
blocks.end: So a fast identification could come from the word’s own history or from what happened just before it.

blocks.main: **Frequency effects can be explained by experience tuning up a word’s activation dynamics.** Most models of this kind assume that activation unfolds over time. Words encountered more often are tuned to be more sensitive, so they are easier to activate.
sub: Every encounter with a word might raise its **baseline** (resting) level of activation.
It might strengthen the word’s incoming connections, so the word is activated more quickly.
It might change a **threshold** parameter, so less activation is needed to recognize the word.
Rumelhart and McClelland’s 1986 Interactive Activation model, with its plot of CAVE rising above competing words, is one model that simulates frequency effects.
blocks.end: So the frequency effect is a very simple form of learning built into how activation rises.

blocks.main: **Repetition priming happens because activation falls off more slowly than it rises.** Activation does not rise and fall instantaneously. If a word is seen again while its activation is still high from the last exposure, its starting point is already higher than usual.
sub: So the word needs less new input to reach recognition.
This is repetition priming, a basic effect in psychology.
blocks.end: So leftover activation from the first exposure gives the second exposure a head start.

questions.q: How is “associated” different from “similar”?
questions.a: Two words are associated when one tends to bring the other to mind, and similar when they share properties. TIGER and STRIPES are associated, but a tiger and a stripe are not similar things. LION and TIGER are both similar animals and associated words.

questions.q: Describe how a simple lexical network identifies the word LION in the perceptual identification task.
questions.a: The LION node is weakly activated when the word contrasts poorly with a noise mask. As the word becomes clearer, its activation increases. When the signal-to-noise ratio is very favorable, activation is strong enough to count as identification, and the participant pushes the button.

questions.q: Give three ways experience could produce a frequency effect in an activation model.
questions.a: Each encounter with a word might raise its baseline level of activation, so it starts closer to recognition. It might strengthen the incoming connections, so the word is activated more quickly. It might change a threshold parameter, so less activation is needed for recognition.

questions.q: Why does seeing a word again shortly afterward make it faster to identify?
questions.a: It is faster because activation falls off more slowly than it rises. When the word appears again, some activation from the first exposure is still there, so its baseline is higher than usual. The word needs less new input to be identified, and this is repetition priming.

questions.q: What did Hubel and Weisel (1968) find, and why does it matter for psycholinguistics?
questions.a: Hubel and Weisel (1968) found simple cells in primary visual cortex that respond to lines of particular orientations in a particular receptive field. One cell responds most strongly to upward movement of a line at about 315°, so it represents that combination of features. Psycholinguistics extends this idea of activation to perceptual and conceptual representations.

title: Spreading activation, mediated priming and learning

blocks.main: **Spreading activation explains how one word can prime a different, related word.** Two effects need more than single nodes. These are **neighborhood effects** (effects of how similar a word is to other words) and associative, semantic or phonological priming. Both require the nodes in the network to be connected.
sub: Connection strengths between nodes are set by their association, as measured in the norms.
So when “lion” is activated, some of that activation travels along a weighted connection to “tiger.”
This is the spreading activation account of **semantic priming** (faster recognition of a word after a related word).
blocks.end: So a related prime gives the target a head start before the target even appears.

blocks.main: **Mediated priming is priming between two words that are linked only through a third word.** STRIPES and LION are not directly associated. STRIPES is linked to TIGER, and TIGER is linked to LION. Because activity flows throughout the network, activating “stripes” can still prime “lion.”
sub: In the demonstration, STRIPES and then LION emerge gradually from a noise mask, as in a perceptual identification trial.
This kind of finding is very representative of psycholinguistics, with careful study design and small effects.
The result is counterintuitive, because there is no obvious reason stripes should prime lion except through tiger.
blocks.end: So mediated priming is compelling evidence that activation really spreads through a network.

blocks.main: **Balota and Lorch found mediated priming when people read the target aloud, but not in lexical decision.** Their prime and target, such as lion and stripes, were related only through a mediating concept, tiger. In **lexical decision** (judging whether a string is a word), directly related pairs like lion and tiger were faster, but mediated pairs were not.
sub: In **pronunciation** (reading the target aloud), both directly related and mediated pairs were faster than neutral or unrelated primes.
The mediated benefit was small but appeared at both prime-to-target delays.
They concluded that activation spreads beyond directly related concepts, and that features of the lexical decision task masked the mediated effect.
blocks.end: So whether a small priming effect appears can depend on the task used to measure it.

blocks.main: **Bottom-up processing builds words from features, and top-down processing lets word knowledge shape how letters are seen.** In the Interactive Activation network, feature detectors activate letter nodes, and letter nodes activate word nodes such as WORK, WORD, WEAR and WEAK. Activation for a word then feeds back down to the letters that fit it.
sub: When the last letter of WORK is partly hidden, activation for WORK changes how that letter is interpreted.
This top-down influence is one way of modeling **pattern completion**, which Menn discusses at length.
blocks.end: So recognition combines evidence from the input with expectations from stored words.

blocks.main: **Associative learning explains how these networks get into the brain.** The simple, powerful idea is that “neurons that fire together, wire together.” This is **Hebbian learning**, in which units active at the same time strengthen their connection.
sub: These mechanisms were historically considered insufficient to learn anything important about language.
More recent arguments are about what role they play and how innate knowledge constrains them. This matters because large language models learn many structural features of language this way.
To generalize, an associative model must represent similarity, so it uses **distributed representations** (patterns of activity across many units).
So what you know about robins and canaries can generalize to new birds as you learn about them.
blocks.end: So activation, spreading activation, top-down processing, associative learning and distributed representations together form the toolkit for modeling lexical networks.

questions.q: Why do neighborhood effects and related-word priming require adding connections to a network?
questions.a: They require connections because they involve one word changing the activity of a different word. A single isolated node can only explain changes in its own activity, as in repetition priming. Weighted connections let activation travel from a prime like lion to a related word like tiger.

questions.q: What is mediated priming, and why is it strong evidence for spreading activation?
questions.a: Mediated priming is priming between two words that are linked only through a third word, such as lion and stripes through tiger. Lion and stripes are not directly associated, so a direct association cannot explain the effect. The effect only makes sense if activation spreads onward through the network.

questions.q: What did Balota and Lorch find in lexical decision and in pronunciation?
questions.a: In lexical decision, directly related primes helped but mediated primes did not. In pronunciation, both directly related and mediated primes helped compared with neutral and unrelated primes. They concluded that activation does spread beyond directly related concepts, and that the lexical decision task masked the mediated effect.

questions.q: What is the difference between bottom-up and top-down processing in the Interactive Activation model?
questions.a: Bottom-up processing sends activation from visual features to letters and then to words. Top-down processing sends activation from a word like WORK back down to the letters that fit it. This feedback helps complete a partly hidden letter, which is a model of pattern completion.

questions.q: Why do associative models need distributed representations?
questions.a: They need them because an associative model must represent similarity in order to generalize. In a distributed representation, similar items share parts of their activity pattern. So what is learned about robins and canaries can carry over to a new bird.

title: Localization of language, from phrenology to Lichtheim’s house

blocks.main: **Phrenology was an early attempt to relate brain structure to function by measuring skulls.** It rested on three premises. Different parts of the brain do different processes, aptitude is related to the size of brain regions, and region size shapes the skull.
sub: Its first problem was **inappropriate anatomical measurement**, because skull shape is not a sensitive measure of brain shape.

Its second problem was an **unconstrained definition of functions**. Researchers studied prisoners to locate “criminality,” and women with different numbers of children to locate “philopropogenitiveness.”
blocks.end: So phrenology failed on both the anatomy and the definition of the functions, even though its first premise is not obviously wrong.

blocks.main: **Flourens used experimental lesions to argue against phrenology.** Working mainly with pigeons and rabbits, he established distinct functions for the cerebral cortex, the cerebellum and midbrain structures. He failed to find any match between specific cortical regions and specific senses.
sub: He insisted that the size of the lesion was what mattered.
When most of the cortex was removed, sight, hearing and the other senses disappeared together.
blocks.end: So Flourens argued that the cortex worked as a whole rather than as a map of separate sense centers.

blocks.main: **In 1861, Broca presented the case of “Tan,” who had lost the ability to speak after a brain injury decades earlier.** Tan could only produce one jargon syllable. He otherwise seemed to be “in possession of his senses,” and he seemed to understand what was said.
sub: Tan’s brain had a large lesion that definitely included the third convolution of the frontal lobe, the **inferior frontal gyrus**.
This gave us **Broca’s area**, a portion of the left frontal lobe that is important for speech.
Hughlings Jackson (1874) objected that “to locate the damage which destroys speech and to locate speech are two different things.”
blocks.end: So Tan linked a specific injury to a specific loss, but the damaged site is not necessarily where speech itself is located.

blocks.main: **Lichtheim’s house model explains different aphasias as damage to centers or to the pathways between them.** In the 1870s, German neurologists including Lichtheim and Wernicke made more systematic observations of aphasia. They ascribed specific losses of function to “disconnections” between “centers.”
sub: Sound comes in along the acoustic pathway, a, to **A**, the center for sound images.
**A** connects up to **B**, the center for concepts, so heard words can be understood.
**B** connects down to **M**, the center for movement images, so ideas can be spoken.
**M** sends commands out along the motor pathway, m, and a direct path from A to M allows verbatim repetition.
So a disconnection between A and B could cause a loss of understanding of spoken words. A disconnection between A and M could cause a loss of repetition.
blocks.end: So each numbered break in the house predicts a different form of aphasia, and this center-based approach is an ancestor of modularity.

blocks.main: **Freud criticized the diagram-drawing school as naïve.** In his early neurological research, he doubted that the brain is organized by psychological categories like “word forms” or “concepts.” He proposed instead that language emerged from “fields” connecting perceptual and motor abilities to “drives.”
blocks.end: So Freud raised a lasting question in cognitive neuroscience, whether brain areas really match our descriptions of cognitive functions.

blocks.main: **MRI of Broca’s original brains revealed that the damage was much deeper and wider than Broca’s area.** Dronkers and colleagues found that Leborgne’s lesion was very deep and included the **insula**. There was also heavy white matter damage to the **superior longitudinal fasciculus**, which connects the front and back of the cerebral cortex.
sub: Other work by this group suggests that the insula, not Broca’s area, is strongly associated with **speech apraxia**, the condition Broca described.
Broca’s behavioral description was crude, because linguistics then focused on history and experimental psychology had not been invented.
His anatomy was also crude and probably wrong, because detailed cortical maps came later, and Brodmann’s map appeared only in 1909.
Others such as the Daxes and Wernicke showed similar things, and Wernicke’s fluent patient produced meaningless gibberish.
blocks.end: So we still talk about Broca because his case made relating specific functions to specific brain regions a respectable pursuit.

questions.q: What were phrenology’s premises, and which ones were wrong?
questions.a: Phrenology assumed that brain parts do different processes, that aptitude depends on region size, and that region size shapes the skull. The idea that different brain parts do different things is not obviously wrong. The method failed because skull shape is not a sensitive measure of brain shape and the functions, like “criminality,” were not properly defined.

questions.q: What did Broca observe in Tan, and what did Hughlings Jackson object?
questions.a: Broca observed that Tan could produce only one jargon syllable but seemed to understand what was said. Tan’s brain had a large lesion including the left inferior frontal gyrus, which became Broca’s area. Hughlings Jackson (1874) objected that locating the damage that destroys speech is not the same as locating speech.

questions.q: Explain Lichtheim’s house model and two disconnections it predicts.
questions.a: Lichtheim’s house has a center for sound images (A), a center for concepts (B) and a center for movement images (M), joined by pathways. A disconnection between A and B predicts a loss of understanding of spoken words. A disconnection between A and M predicts a loss of verbatim repetition.

questions.q: What was Freud’s critique of the aphasia diagram-makers?
questions.a: Freud argued that it was naïve to expect the brain to be organized by psychological categories like word forms or concepts. He proposed instead that language came from fields connecting perceptual and motor abilities to drives. His critique raises the lasting question of whether brain areas match cognitive functions.

questions.q: What did Dronkers and colleagues find when they scanned Broca’s cases?
questions.a: They found that the lesion was very deep, including the insula, with heavy white matter damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus. Their other work links speech apraxia, the condition Broca described, to the insula rather than Broca’s area. So Broca’s original localization was probably wrong.

title: Lesion studies, neuroimaging and subtraction logic

blocks.main: **Cognitive neuropsychology depends on cognitive psychology to define the functions it tests.** Much of what we learned about structure and function in the twentieth century came from experiments with brain-damaged individuals. Theory supplies hypotheses about which operations might be separable, such as recognizing the abstract forms of words and computing their meaning.
sub: Quantitative measurements allow statistical comparison, which is critical because deficits are rarely complete.
Anatomical imaging, such as the scan of H.M.’s middle temporal lobes, locates injuries without waiting for autopsy.
But studies of brain-injured patients show what behavior looks like after damage, so they tell us only indirectly what the intact region does.
blocks.end: So Hughlings Jackson’s warning still applies even with modern scans.

blocks.main: **Metabolic imaging such as PET and fMRI studies brains in action, but it measures an indirect index.** The PET studies described by Posner and colleagues used radio-labeled oxygen as a marker for activity. These methods track oxygen consumption, not neural activity itself.
sub: They are slow, because metabolic processes unfold over seconds while important neural events take milliseconds or less.
They have only fair spatial resolution, in millimeters, while important events happen at the micron scale.
There is activity all over the brain all the time, so a task must be compared with a **control condition**.
This **subtraction logic** takes the task image minus the control image to isolate the operation that differs between them.
blocks.end: So an activation map is only meaningful relative to a carefully chosen control.

blocks.main: **Posner and colleagues used subtraction to localize semantic processing of words, and the region roughly matched Broca’s area.** They compared monitoring visual words for dangerous animals with passive viewing. They also compared generating uses for words with simply repeating them, for visual and for auditory words.
sub: All three semantic contrasts activated the left inferior prefrontal cortex.
They concluded that the PET data support localizing operations on visual, phonological and semantic codes.
Whole tasks like word reading or shifting attention are not performed by any single brain area, because each involves many component computations.
blocks.end: So the answer to “is this better than phrenology?” rests on defining component operations carefully and testing them with controlled contrasts.

blocks.main: **Language has turned up at key moments in debates about localization of function.** Broca’s presentation of Tan helped establish **lesion-behavior analysis**. Some of the very first PET and fMRI studies used activation of Broca’s area in language tasks as evidence that cognitive functions could be localized.
blocks.end: So language is well suited to these studies because it breaks into distinct abilities, like speaking, understanding and repeating, that can be measured separately.

questions.q: Why does cognitive neuropsychology depend on cognitive psychology?
questions.a: It depends on cognitive psychology for definitions of the functions being tested. Theory says which operations might be separable, such as recognizing word forms and computing meaning. Quantitative measures then let those operations be compared statistically, which matters because deficits are rarely complete.

questions.q: What are three limits of metabolic imaging like PET and fMRI?
questions.a: First, they are metabolic, so they measure an index of oxygen consumption rather than neural activity. Second, they are slow, because metabolic changes take seconds while neural events take milliseconds. Third, their spatial resolution is in millimeters, while important events happen at the micron scale.

questions.q: How did Posner and colleagues use subtraction logic to isolate semantic processing?
questions.a: They subtracted a control task from a semantic task that differed only in needing word meaning. Monitoring words for dangerous animals was compared with passive viewing, and generating uses was compared with repeating words. The left inferior frontal region active in all three semantic contrasts corresponded roughly to Broca’s area.

questions.q: Is PET localization better than phrenology?
questions.a: It is better because it localizes carefully defined component operations, not broad traits, and it uses controlled task contrasts. Posner and colleagues argued that operations on visual, phonological and semantic codes are localized. They also argued that whole tasks like reading are not done by any single area.

title: Behaviorism, AI and Chomsky’s Cognitive Revolution

blocks.main: **The Cognitive Revolution brought back the idea of language as a formal, symbolic system.** Experimental psychology in the 1950s and 1960s was actively hostile to talking about internal states. **Skinner’s** Verbal Behavior tried to explain how language is learned by **operant conditioning**. **Chomsky’s (1959)** review of the book is better remembered than the book itself.
sub: The formal tradition connects to artificial intelligence, which dates back to the beginning of the digital computer.
Computers were the first machines that did so many kinds of calculations and logical operations, so people asked how they differed from human intelligence.
blocks.end: So the revolution made internal rules and representations legitimate parts of a theory of language.

blocks.main: **The Turing test asks whether a computer can replace a person in a conversation game without the examiner noticing.** In the imitation game, A and B are a man and a woman, and C is an examiner who must figure out their genders. A tries to fool C, and B tries to help C.
sub: If a computer replaces A or B and C does not notice, the computer has shown “intelligence.”
The test depends on natural language and on deception.
Turing explicitly excluded expert behaviors like calculating large sums or composing poetry.
He concluded that the best route to an intelligent machine is to build one with a child’s capabilities. It would then learn to be more like an adult.
blocks.end: So Turing tied intelligence to ordinary conversation and learning rather than to expert skills.

blocks.main: **Early AI, called GOFAI, solved formal problems by applying procedures to symbols.** Newell and Simon’s **General Problem Solver** took an abstract description of a problem and applied procedures to symbols to find a solution. It was very good at games and puzzles like the Tower of Hanoi and chess, and at geometry proofs and algebra word problems.
sub: Technology favored formal problems, because input was limited to punchcards and machine language. There was no way to give a computer an image and ask it to find the face.
Theory also favored them, because rational behavior was taken as the model of intelligence.
A trained pigeon can guide a missile without knowing what it is doing. AI programs at least represent goal states and choose procedures to reach them.
blocks.end: So early AI treated intelligence as rational symbol manipulation.

blocks.main: **Chomsky argued that a speaker’s knowledge is an internalized grammar, a set of abstract rules that produce grammatical sentences.** There are an infinite number of grammatical sentences. We can still judge whether any new sentence is grammatical, which is remarkable. So people’s **grammaticality judgments** became the key data for the study of language.
sub: In behaviorism, **stimulus generalization** spreads a response to similar stimuli. A pigeon trained to peck for a green light also pecks for similar colors.
That kind of generalization depends on concrete similarity, such as color or number.
Grammatical sentences have no obvious similarity to one another, so generalization cannot explain how we recognize new ones.
Chomsky added that all normal children acquire comparably complex grammars remarkably fast, which suggests humans are specially designed to do this.
blocks.end: So we recognize a new sentence because our grammar generates it, not because it resembles sentences we have heard.

blocks.main: **Chomsky attacked stimulus control, the idea that the environment determines what a speaker says.** For Skinner, saying “Mozart” in response to a piece of music is an example of stimulus control. Chomsky objected that “we do not know what the current stimuli are until he responds.”
sub: So Skinner was posing the wrong question. Why people say what they do depends on social interactions, cognitive processes and past experience, much of it unrelated to language.
The tractable problem is to study the structure of what people say and derive the rules that produce it.
Neither “colorless green ideas sleep furiously” nor “furiously sleep ideas green colorless” had ever been heard, yet only the first is grammatical (Chomsky, 1955).
“Car! Getting towed! Yours!” is ungrammatical even though the stimulus that controlled it is perfectly clear.
blocks.end: So grammaticality depends on structure, not on past experience or on the stimulus.

questions.q: What is stimulus control, and why did Chomsky reject it as an explanation of language?
questions.a: Stimulus control is Skinner’s idea that an aspect of the environment controls a verbal response, like music prompting “Mozart.” Chomsky objected that we cannot know what the controlling stimulus was until the person responds. So the account cannot predict anything, and he argued the real question is the structure of what people say.

questions.q: Why can’t stimulus generalization explain how we recognize new sentences?
questions.a: Stimulus generalization depends on concrete similarity, such as a pigeon pecking for colors close to green. Grammatical sentences have no obvious similarity to one another. So there is no dimension along which a new sentence resembles old ones, and Chomsky argued that an internalized grammar generates it instead.

questions.q: What does “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” tell us about grammar?
questions.a: It tells us that grammaticality does not depend on meaning or past experience. Neither that sentence nor its reversed version had been heard before, yet only the original is grammatical. “Car! Getting towed! Yours!” is clear in context but ungrammatical, so a clear stimulus does not make a sentence grammatical.

questions.q: Describe the Turing test and its notable features.
questions.a: In the imitation game, an examiner tries to tell the genders of two hidden players, one of whom tries to fool him. A computer counts as intelligent if it replaces a player without the examiner noticing. The test relies on natural language and deception and excludes expert skills, and Turing suggested building a child-like machine that learns.

questions.q: Why did early AI focus on formal problems?
questions.a: It focused on them partly because of technology, since input was limited to punchcards and machine language. It also focused on them for theoretical reasons, because rational behavior was seen as the model of intelligence. Programs like the General Problem Solver represented goals and chose procedures to reach them.

title: Marr’s levels and the emergentist alternative

blocks.main: **Marr described cognitive systems at three levels of analysis, computational, algorithmic and implementational.** Chomsky was describing language at the **computational level**. A cash register makes the levels concrete.
sub: At the computational level, a cash register takes prices and determines the amount due, then takes a payment and computes the change.
At the algorithmic level, it uses addition for the price and subtraction for the change.
At the implementational level, the hardware does not matter, so a credit card reader or a computer program are also “cash registers.”
blocks.end: So the levels separate what a system computes, how it computes it, and what physically does the work.

blocks.main: **Treating language as a Type I problem means studying grammar without worrying about how the brain implements it.** Marr called problems that break down cleanly into his levels “Type I” problems. For language, this means working at the computational level of Universal Grammar and the algorithmic level of specific processes.
sub: The implementational level, with errors, memory limitations and associative learning, is set aside.
Marr equated Chomsky’s “competence” theory with a computational theory.
In a **Type 2** problem, many processes act at once, and their interaction is its own simplest description.
If language is a Type 2 problem, details about how it is implemented in the brain might be unavoidable in a theory of language.
blocks.end: So a whole alternative approach to language research is built on the idea that implementation matters.

blocks.main: **Emergentist and parallel distributed processing approaches make their strong commitments at the implementational level.** They use **distributed representations**, like activity patterns over groups of neurons. They assume **gradual learning**, like adjusting the strength of synaptic connections.
sub: **Elman (1990)** built **simple recurrent networks** whose only job is to predict the next item they will see, and they learn this gradually.
A letter-prediction network found the words in an unspaced text like “manyyearsagoaboyandgirl,” because its prediction error goes down within words.
Trained on simple sentences, a similar network grouped words into grammatical classes and even some semantic categories, as a side effect of learning to predict.
blocks.end: So word boundaries and word classes can emerge from prediction without being built in as rules.

blocks.main: **Statistical models trained on large corpora can tell “colorless green ideas sleep furiously” from its reversal.** Norvig pointed out that every two-word part of the sentence had appeared in published text before 1955. **Pereira (2001)** trained a statistical finite-state model, with word categories, on newspaper text.
sub: That model computed that the grammatical order is 200,000 times more probable than the reversed order.
Many engineering solutions in natural language processing work this way.
blocks.end: So statistics over experience can capture a judgment Chomsky treated as needing an internal grammar.

blocks.main: **Two traditions in psycholinguistics differ in what they assume linguistic knowledge is.** The **GOFAI, modular or Chomskyan** tradition assumes knowledge is abstract, symbolic and different in kind from other knowledge. Its job is to study how that knowledge interfaces with messy perception, motor control and memory.
sub: The **emergentist or functionalist** tradition assumes rule-like behavior emerges from statistical learning, and that perception and cognition shape linguistic representations.
Its job is to study language use and relate it to general psychology.
Messiness is everywhere, from probabilistic phonetic categories to ambiguous words, past tense exceptions like RUN and RAN, and syntactic variation.
**Moravec’s paradox** says theorem proving is easy for computers but recognizing a face is hard, while the opposite is true for humans.
blocks.end: So characterizing language in formal terms, as for a computer program, may be a false trail.

blocks.main: **Fixed categories and rules are often fuzzy in practice.** Wittgenstein (1953) noted that games share no single defining feature. Instead they form **family resemblances**, overlapping similarities that cross from one member to another.
sub: Many phenomena in language are probabilistic in the same way.
Roger Shepard studied perception, Eleanor Rosch studied categorization, and Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied decision making. Their results made cognition seem less formal and rational.
blocks.end: So similarity-based generalization and hunches became serious alternatives to formal rules.

questions.q: Explain Marr’s three levels using the cash register.
questions.a: At the computational level, a cash register determines the amount due and the change. At the algorithmic level, it does this with addition and subtraction. At the implementational level, the hardware does not matter, so a card reader or a program can be a cash register too.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Type I and a Type 2 problem, and why does it matter for language?
questions.a: A Type I problem breaks down cleanly, so its computation can be studied without its implementation. A Type 2 problem is solved by many interacting processes whose interaction is its own simplest description. If language is Type 2, brain implementation becomes unavoidable in a theory of language.

questions.q: What did Elman’s simple recurrent networks learn from predicting the next item?
questions.a: A letter-prediction network found word boundaries in unspaced text, because its prediction error dropped within words. A network trained on simple sentences grouped words into grammatical classes and some semantic categories. Both results arose as side effects of prediction, not from built-in rules.

questions.q: Contrast the two traditions in psycholinguistics.
questions.a: The GOFAI or Chomskyan tradition treats linguistic knowledge as abstract, symbolic and unlike other knowledge, and studies its interface with perception and memory. The emergentist tradition treats rules as emerging from statistical learning shaped by perception and cognition. It studies language use and relates it to general psychology.

title: Speech errors as evidence and the kinds of slips

blocks.main: **Speech errors are evidence about the units and processes of speech planning.** Fromkin titled her article “Speech errors as linguistic evidence.” This was gutsy for a linguist, because errors belong to performance rather than the idealized knowledge linguists usually study.
sub: Spreading activation models explain errors with four ideas.
**Noise** in the activation of different parts of the system can push the wrong item forward.
**Frequency** matters, because common words are easier to activate.
**Other sources of activation** include what you just said, what you plan to say, and what you are trying not to say.
**Similarity** matters, because activation spreads more easily between items related in meaning, syntax or sound.
blocks.end: So an error happens when a competing item gets more activation than the intended one.

blocks.main: **A tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state is partial activation of a word’s meaning and sound that falls short of the threshold for producing it.** In the study reviewed by Lise Abrams, people were asked for the word meaning goods traded illegally, which is “contraband.” Those in a TOT state then read a list containing words that shared the first, middle or last syllable of the target, or no syllable.
sub: People resolved their TOT states most often after words sharing the first syllable, such as “contact.”
Priming helps because the shared sounds add activation to the missing word form.
blocks.end: So a related sound can push a partly active word over the threshold for speaking.

blocks.main: **Slips of the tongue differ in the direction the misplaced sound travels.** In **anticipation**, a later sound comes in too early, as in “week long race” becoming “reek long race.” In **perseveration**, an earlier sound repeats too late, as in “John gave the boy” becoming “John gave the goy.” In **metathesis**, two sounds swap places, as in “keep a tape” becoming “teep a cape.”
sub: Dr. Spooner supposedly once said “Mardon me padam, this pie is occupewed. Can I sew you to another sheet?”
Anticipations come from activation of what you are planning to say.
Perseverations come from activation that remains from what you just said.
blocks.end: So the direction of a slip points to the source of the competing activation.

blocks.main: **Fromkin’s cluster errors are evidence that single phonemes are units in speech planning.** When her paper was written, there were arguments about whether the phoneme was a unit of planning. It might have turned out that whole consonant clusters always move together, which would give errors like “clesh freer water.”
sub: Instead, clusters get broken up all the time in production.
“Fish grotto” became “frish gotto,” where only the r of the gr cluster moved.
“Fresh clear water” became “flesh queer water,” where only the r and l swapped.
blocks.end: So single segments, not whole clusters, are what move in these errors.

blocks.main: **Slips of the ear are perceptual errors, and they reveal top-down processing.** A **mondegreen** is a misheard phrase, named for hearing “laid him on the green” as “Lady Mondegreen.” Word boundaries are ambiguous, as in “The good candy came anyways” and “The good can decay many ways.” So context matters, especially in songs where prosody helps less.
sub: A **malapropism** is a perceptual error, because the speaker says exactly what they intend.
The speaker heard a word like “congenital” and decided the intended word was a more familiar one, “congenial.”
Many speech errors go undetected for the same top-down reasons.
Some “errors” are deliberate, like “The upper hand is on the other foot,” which is memorable because it blends two familiar expressions.
blocks.end: So our expectations fill in what we hear, which explains both mishearings and unnoticed slips.

questions.q: Why should speech errors be of interest to psycholinguists?
questions.a: Speech errors are of interest because their form reveals the units and processes of speech planning. Fromkin’s title, “Speech errors as linguistic evidence,” was gutsy because errors belong to performance, not idealized knowledge. Errors that break clusters apart, for instance, are evidence that phonemes are planning units.

questions.q: What four aspects of spreading activation help explain speech errors?
questions.a: Noise in the activation of the system can let the wrong item win. Frequency matters because common words are easier to activate. Other sources of activation, like what was just said or is planned next, add competitors, and similarity lets activation spread to related items.

questions.q: What is a tip-of-the-tongue state, and why might priming help?
questions.a: A TOT state is partial activation of a word’s meaning and sound that falls short of the threshold for producing it. Priming helps because words sharing the target’s sounds add activation to its form. Resolution was highest after words sharing the first syllable of the target.

questions.q: Distinguish anticipation, perseveration and metathesis with an example of each.
questions.a: Anticipation brings a later sound in too early, as in “reek long race” for “week long race.” Perseveration repeats an earlier sound too late, as in “John gave the goy.” Metathesis swaps two sounds, as in “teep a cape” for “keep a tape.”

questions.q: Why are malapropisms perceptual errors rather than speech errors?
questions.a: They are perceptual errors because the speaker says exactly what they intend. The speaker earlier heard an unfamiliar word like “congenital” and decided it must have been a familiar one, “congenial.” This is top-down processing at work in perception.

title: The production model and the functional level

blocks.main: **The basic model of speech production turns a message into speech through a series of levels.** The levels are **Message**, **Functional**, **Positional**, **Phonological Encoding** and **Speech Gesture**. An early version comes from Fromkin (1971), whose utterance generator runs from the “meaning” to be conveyed down to motor commands to the muscles.
sub: The message level decides what to say.
The functional level selects lemmas and assigns them semantic roles.
The positional level builds a syntactic frame with slots for those lemmas.
Phonological encoding turns the result into a string of phonemes.
The speech gesture level executes that string as movements.
blocks.end: So each kind of speech error can be traced to the level where it went wrong.

blocks.main: **The message level is what the speaker intends to convey, and it is hard to study experimentally.** Take “I won a bunch of money on the game Sunday.” You would say it differently to a fan of the losing team, to someone who ignores football, and in a tweet. The event stays the same while the message changes with the audience.
sub: Some studies try to control the message with an elicitation paradigm, such as the picture book “Frog, where are you?”
Even then, the intended message can depend on age, culture and audience.
blocks.end: So the message level remains somewhat mysterious.

blocks.main: **At the functional level we select lemmas, not finished words.** A **lemma** is a word’s abstract identity before its grammatical form is fixed. The error “Where’d I bring it when I put it in” was meant to be “Where’d I put it when I brought it in.”
sub: The verbs switched places, but the produced forms reflect a tense change applied later.
If the finished word “brought” had been selected, it would have moved as “brought.”
Instead the lemma BRING was selected and later expressed in the present form its new position required.
blocks.end: So word identity is chosen before its grammatical form.

blocks.main: **People often say the opposite of what they mean because antonyms are similar at many levels.** Antonyms are semantically related and strongly associated, which is a perfect storm in the spreading activation framework. They can also take the same semantic roles and belong to the same word class.
sub: Because they fit the same roles and slots, the rest of the production system can handle the wrong one smoothly.
So it is easy for activation to spread from a lemma to its antonym, and for the antonym to win.
blocks.end: So a big change in meaning can come out as a small, grammatical substitution.

blocks.main: **A blend mixes two competing words into one form.** Lewis Carroll deliberately built “frumious” from “fuming” and “furious.” Spontaneous blends happen when two alternatives, such as “mainly” and “mostly,” are active at the same moment.
sub: Blends happen “where there are a number of alternative possibilities.”
In speech production there are almost always alternative possibilities, so competition is a normal part of speaking.
blocks.end: So blends are direct evidence that more than one candidate is active during word selection.

blocks.main: **The functional level slots lemmas into semantic roles.** In “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me” and “I have eaten the plums in the icebox,” the roles are the same. The verb is TO EAT, the Agent is ME and the Undergoer is PLUM.
sub: Arranging these roles in different orders has syntactic consequences, such as whether ME comes out as “I” or “me.”
That arrangement happens later, at the positional level.
By the end of the functional level we have decided on a message, selected lemmas and associated them with semantic roles.
blocks.end: So we are still nowhere near putting a clause together, much less saying it out loud.

questions.q: Why can’t we say that we select “words” at the functional level?
questions.a: We cannot say this because of the error “Where’d I bring it when I put it in.” The speaker meant “Where’d I put it when I brought it in.” The verbs swapped, but bring appeared in the form its new slot required. So the abstract lemma BRING was selected, and its tense was applied later.

questions.q: Why do people so often say the opposite of what they mean?
questions.a: Antonyms are semantically related and strongly associated, so activation spreads easily from a lemma to its antonym. They also take the same semantic roles and belong to the same word class. So the rest of the production system handles the wrong word smoothly.

questions.q: What has been decided by the end of the functional level?
questions.a: By the end of the functional level, the speaker has decided on a message to convey. Appropriate lemmas have been selected and associated with semantic roles such as Agent and Undergoer. No clause has been built yet, and nothing has been said out loud.

questions.q: Why is the message level hard to study?
questions.a: It is hard to study because the same event is expressed differently depending on audience and purpose. Winning money on a game would be told differently to a losing fan, a non-fan, or in a tweet. Elicitation tools like “Frog, where are you?” control what people see but not what message they intend.

questions.q: What do blends reveal about speech production?
questions.a: Blends reveal that two alternatives can be active at the same time during word selection. Material from both words, like “mainly” and “mostly,” ends up in one form. Since there are almost always alternatives in speech, competition is a normal part of speaking.

title: The positional level, phonological encoding and gestures

blocks.main: **The positional level builds a syntactic frame with slots for the lemmas chosen at the functional level.** Take “Where’d I bring it when I put it in?” The functional level supplies two verbs, PUT and BRING, with I/ME as Agent and IT as Undergoer of both. The positional level must also express the temporal relationship between the verbs.
sub: The frame is “Where’d I [verb, root form] it when I [verb, past] it in?”
The first clause requires the base form, because of the question structure with an auxiliary verb.
The next clause requires the past form.
The error arose while the slots were being filled, so BRING landed in the base-form slot and came out as “bring.”
blocks.end: So the frame decides the form of a word, and the lemma decides which word fills it.

blocks.main: **Stranded affixes stay in their slot while the roots move, so affixes must be represented separately.** In “a language needer learns,” meant as “a language learner needs,” two lemmas switched while the positional level stayed the same. The noun is a verb plus the derivational affix -er, so -er stayed in the noun slot and attached to NEED.
sub: “He did that easy enoughly,” meant as “easily enough,” also has a stranded affix, because -ly makes an adjective into an adverb.
In this case something also went wrong while setting up the positional frame, so the adverb slot ended up second and enough received the -ly.
Errors produce non-words like “needer” and “enoughly” on the fly, which a lexicon of stored related words could not do.
blocks.end: So lemmas and affixes are represented separately, affixes have slots, and derived words can be built by a grammatical process.

blocks.main: **Phonological encoding turns the lemmas, affixes and particles into an ordered string of phonemes.** A positional instruction like “add -er” still leaves sound work to do. Easy /’i.zi/ becomes easily /’i.zIl.i/, and enough /i.’nəf/ becomes enoughly /i.’nəf.li/, while vowels and stress can shift as in certification.
sub: In “easy enoughly,” phonological encoding worked fine, because the speaker did not say something like “easy /inəvɪli/.”
Errors at this level are problems with the ordering of phonemes.
Examples are “fish grotto” becoming “gish frotto” and “Chomsky and Halle” becoming “Chomsky and Challe.”
Another is “with this ring I do wed” becoming “with this wing I do red.”
Menn describes these errors as “neat,” because they follow English phonotactics and are clearly produced.
blocks.end: So phonological encoding errors are clean rearrangements of real phonemes.

blocks.main: **The speech gesture level turns the planned phonemes into movements executed by the motor system.** Unlike phonological encoding errors, gestural errors are not necessarily neat. They produce unclear or imprecise speech.
sub: Many errors are ambiguous, such as “ad hoc” /æd hɑk/ coming out as “odd hack” /ɑd hæk/.
It could be metathesis at the phonological encoding level, or a miscuing of tongue position at the gestural level.
blocks.end: So a neat error points to encoding and a sloppy one points to gestures, but some errors fit both.

blocks.main: **Collected errors can be sorted by the level of representation that changed.** “Buyed in” for “bought in” regularizes an irregular past tense. “Wash my teeth and brush my face” exchanges two verbs while their objects stay put. “Following vowel” becoming “vollowing fowel” exchanges initial consonants. “Seat heaters” becoming “heat seaters” moves seat and heat while the ending stays with the second word.
sub: “Lana del Rey” becoming “Marina del Rey” substitutes a familiar name.
“For all intensive purposes” replaces part of a familiar expression, like a malapropism.
“Law and Order SUV” reorders the letters of SVU into a familiar abbreviation.
“He cooked his kitchen” replaces chicken with a word that shares its sounds and fits the cooking context.
blocks.end: So placing an error in the model means comparing the intended and produced forms at each level.

blocks.main: **Observational studies of speech errors are limited by the observer’s attention and perception.** What collectors listen for, and their expectations from the model, can change what they hear and report. Reconstructing an error also needs information about the situation, such as the intended message.
sub: People are not very good at hearing sounds “halfway” between two phonemes, especially consonants.
People are biased against perceiving phonotactically illegal strings.
People are biased toward hearing ambiguous sounds as words, so a sound between “giss” and “kiss” sounds more like “kiss.”
This is **theory-dependent observation**, so whole classes of errors might be missed.
blocks.end: So experimental methods and careful measurement are needed, though they fix only some of these problems.

questions.q: What happens at the positional level?
questions.a: The positional level builds a syntactic structure with slots for the lemmas from the functional level, plus the particles the grammar requires. It also fixes the form each slot needs, such as base form or past tense. Errors like “Where’d I bring it when I put it in” arise while these slots are being filled.

questions.q: How is “a language needer learns” similar to and different from “Where’d I bring it when I put it in”?
questions.a: It is similar because two lemmas switched while being fed into the positional level, and the frame stayed the same. It is different because the noun “needer” is a verb plus the derivational affix -er. The -er stayed in its slot and attached to the wrong root.

questions.q: How is “He did that easy enoughly” similar to and different from “a language needer learns”?
questions.a: Both errors have a stranded affix, here -ly, which turns an adjective into an adverb. The difference is that something also went wrong while setting up the positional frame itself. The adverb slot ended up second, so enough received the -ly and easy lost it.

questions.q: What do errors like “needer” and “enoughly” suggest about how words are represented?
questions.a: They suggest that lemmas and affixes are represented separately and that affixes have slots at the positional level. They also suggest that derived words can be produced by a grammatical process. A lexicon of stored related words could not create these non-words on the fly.

questions.q: How do phonological encoding errors differ from speech gesture errors?
questions.a: Phonological encoding errors misorder phonemes but are neat, following English phonotactics and produced clearly. Gesture errors happen in motor execution, so they produce unclear or imprecise speech. Some errors, like “odd hack” for “ad hoc,” could come from either level.

questions.q: Why are observational collections of speech errors biased?
questions.a: They are biased because observers hear what their expectations and perception allow. Listeners miss sounds halfway between phonemes, resist hearing illegal strings, and hear ambiguous sounds as words, like “kiss” for something between “giss” and “kiss.” This theory-dependent observation can hide whole classes of errors.

title: Frequency, length and confounds in experimental design
