blocks.main: **Oldfield and Wingfield (1965) found that people name pictures of common objects faster than pictures of rare ones.** They asked people to name pictures of objects. Naming time fell steadily as the frequency of the name increased, in a **log-linear** relationship (a straight line when frequency is on a log scale).
sub: But frequency is related to word length, even in a tiny sample of objects.
Frequent names tend to be short, so either frequency or length could explain the faster naming.
blocks.end: So the frequency effect started out **confounded** with length, meaning the two varied together.

blocks.main: **In English, frequency drops off steeply and length goes up as frequency goes down.** The 200 most frequent words in an old corpus were put into ten bins of twenty words. Mean frequency drops off very dramatically from the most frequent bin to the next, which is **Zipf’s law** in action.
sub: Length is inversely related to frequency, so the most frequent words are the shortest.
A lexical database lets researchers generate word lists with set frequency and length limits, or look up the properties of an existing list.
Boxplots compare the lengths of the 467 most frequent words with 467 low-frequency words chosen at random.
Fewer than a quarter of the high-frequency words are as long as the median low-frequency word.
blocks.end: So choosing low-frequency words at random will always give longer words.

blocks.main: **The solution is to match the two groups on length while still varying frequency.** Researchers should not select the low-frequency words at random. They pick longish high-frequency words and shortish low-frequency words, so the groups have the same lengths but different frequencies.
sub: Oldfield and Wingfield eventually matched their high- and low-frequency words for length.
They still found a robust frequency effect.
So they concluded that frequency effects are not merely length effects in disguise.
blocks.end: So much of psycholinguistics is an effort to show that an effect is not just an effect of some other confounding variable.

blocks.main: **Careful matching on many dimensions is part of good stimulus design, but it has costs.** Cutler (1981) called making up materials “a confounded nuisance.” **Cortese and Simpson (2000)** matched their words on a wide range of properties.
sub: Fine-grained matching may select odd items whose statistics are unusual.
The frequency and length confound is a fact about English, so avoiding it creates a somewhat artificial set of words.
Matching can also leave very few items, and that study had only ten words per cell.
blocks.end: So matching removes a confound but can make the stimuli less representative of the language.

blocks.main: **Most interesting psycholinguistic effects happen below conscious awareness, so tasks can be simple.** A person naming line drawings is not thinking about word frequency or length. So psycholinguists need less trickery than researchers studying stereotyping or altruism, and norming studies simply ask people to rate words.
sub: Many measures are things participants do not consciously control, such as eye movements, EEG and fMRI.
Brain activity is useful as a **dependent variable** (the measured outcome), not only for what it says about the brain.
If two kinds of stimuli produce different brain responses even without a task, the stimuli are different to the participant.
Reaction time and accuracy are also unlikely to be under direct control in most experiments.
blocks.end: So good measures capture processing that participants cannot strategically change.

blocks.main: **A good idea for an experiment starts by asking whether an effect could just be something else.** The question is “Couldn’t it just be …?” Many features of words are correlated with frequency. These include length, age of acquisition, concreteness or imageability, and “contextual diversity.”
sub: So frequency effects might be a catch-all for these other properties.
Even a simple blocking study involves several processes, including object recognition and response selection.
blocks.end: So each alternative explanation suggests a new experiment to rule it out.

questions.q: What did Oldfield and Wingfield first find, and why was it a problem?
questions.a: Oldfield and Wingfield (1965) found that pictures with more frequent names were named faster, in a log-linear relationship. The problem was that frequent words also tend to be short. So the frequency effect was confounded with length, and length could have explained it.

questions.q: Why will random selection of low-frequency words always produce a length confound?
questions.a: It will because length is inversely related to frequency in English. High-frequency words are generally shorter, and fewer than a quarter of them are as long as the typical low-frequency word. So random low-frequency words will almost always be longer.

questions.q: How do you separate frequency from length, and what happened when Oldfield and Wingfield did it?
questions.a: You choose longish high-frequency words and shortish low-frequency words so that the groups match in length but differ in frequency. Oldfield and Wingfield eventually matched their words this way. They still found a robust frequency effect, so frequency effects are not just length effects in disguise.

questions.q: What are the risks of very fine-grained stimulus matching?
questions.a: Fine matching may pick odd items whose statistics are unusual. Because confounds like frequency and length are real facts about English, avoiding them creates an artificial set of words. It can also leave very few items, such as ten words per cell.

questions.q: Why are measures like eye movements and brain activity valuable dependent variables?
questions.a: They are valuable because participants do not consciously control them. If two kinds of stimuli produce different brain responses even without a task, the stimuli must be different to the participant. Reaction time and accuracy are also rarely under direct control.

title: Cyclic semantic blocking and lemma selection

blocks.main: **Belke, Meyer and Damian (2005) found that people name pictures more slowly when the set is semantically related.** In the **cyclic semantic blocking** paradigm, participants repeatedly name sets of objects. **Homogeneous** (HOM) sets have related names, like duck, mouse, fish and snake. **Heterogeneous** (HET) sets have unrelated names, like duck, saw, chair and bus.
sub: The experiment ran for eight cycles, and every picture was shown in each cycle.
The same item, such as duck, appeared in HOM and HET blocks in alternating cycles.
There is a big **identity priming effect**, because naming gets much faster after the first cycle.
There is also a **semantic blocking effect**, because HOM naming stays slower than HET naming after the first cycle.
blocks.end: So repetition speeds naming while semantic relatedness slows it.

blocks.main: **Spreading activation can slow naming because activation and selection are different processes.** A naïve view predicts that a block of similar pictures should speed naming. But naming requires selecting the correct lemma from a set of active ones.
sub: Activation spreads from duck to fish, so related lemmas all become active.
The **WEAVER++** model says selection time depends on the ratio of the most active lemma’s activity to the total activation of all lemmas.
Feedback from the category level adds activation to all the category members, so the target is a smaller share of the total.
So lemma selection takes longer in a homogeneous block.
WEAVER++ focuses on single words, so its syntactic level holds things like number and gender rather than a positional frame.
blocks.end: So the same spreading activation that helps recognition can create competition in production.

blocks.main: **Belke, Meyer and Damian ruled out visual similarity as the cause of blocking.** Objects in the same category might simply look alike. First, the stimuli were normed so that same-category objects were not more visually similar, on average, than objects from different categories.
sub: Second, a control experiment blocked visual similarity alone and found a different pattern.
In that control, the effect appeared in the first block, while semantic blocking appeared only after the first cycle.
blocks.end: So the blocking effect in Experiment 1 is not likely to come from visual similarity.

blocks.main: **In Experiment 2, eye tracking located the blocking effect at lemma selection.** Hermens and colleagues had shown several objects at once and found no effect. So Belke, Meyer and Damian showed four objects simultaneously and had people name them in order while their eyes were tracked.
sub: **Gaze duration** is how long the eyes stay on an object, and lemma selection is coordinated with eye movements.
**Lag** is the time between the eyes leaving an object and its name starting, when phonological encoding and gesture planning continue without visual support.
Speech duration got shorter over the experiment but showed no blocking effect, which fits the gesture level.
Gaze duration showed a blocking effect, but only after the first cycle, which fits lemma selection.
Lag showed no blocking effect, and its small reverse difference was not significant, which fits phonological encoding.
blocks.end: So the semantic cost shows up only in the measure tied to choosing the word.

blocks.main: **In Experiment 3, the blocking effect generalized to new items from the same categories.** New items were introduced in cycle five. Overall naming slowed down dramatically, and the repetition priming effect went away.
sub: But the blocking effect was still there for the new items.
Comparing the new items with the items in cycle one separates category history from repeating a particular item.
blocks.end: So blocking comes from the category being active, not from repeating specific items.

blocks.main: **Converging controls isolate semantic blocking at lemma selection.** It is not visual recognition, because the stimuli were normed and matched and a control experiment gave a different pattern. It is probably not phonological encoding, because the words are not phonologically similar and gaze duration, not lag, was affected.
sub: It is not just a specific effect of repeating lists, because it generalizes to new items.
blocks.end: So each control removes one alternative, and together they leave lemma selection as the best explanation.

questions.q: Describe the cyclic semantic blocking design and its two main effects.
questions.a: Participants repeatedly named pictures over eight cycles in homogeneous sets with related names or heterogeneous sets with unrelated names. Naming got much faster after the first cycle, which is identity priming. Homogeneous sets stayed slower than heterogeneous sets after the first cycle, which is semantic blocking.

questions.q: How can spreading activation make naming slower instead of faster?
questions.a: Naming requires selecting one lemma from all the active ones. In WEAVER++, selection time depends on the target’s activation relative to the total activation of all lemmas. Related pictures and category feedback add activation to competitors, so the target is a smaller share and selection slows.

questions.q: What did eye tracking in Experiment 2 reveal about where blocking happens?
questions.a: Gaze duration showed a blocking effect after the first cycle, and gaze is coordinated with lemma selection. Lag, which reflects phonological encoding after the eyes move on, showed no significant effect. Speech duration, linked to the gesture level, showed no blocking, so the cost sits at lemma selection.

questions.q: Why does Experiment 3 matter?
questions.a: Experiment 3 matters because blocking survived when new items from the same categories were introduced. Repetition priming disappeared for the new items, but the semantic blocking effect remained. So blocking is not an item-specific effect of repeating lists.

questions.q: How did Belke, Meyer and Damian rule out visual similarity?
questions.a: They normed the stimuli so that same-category objects were not more visually similar than objects from different categories. They also ran a control experiment that blocked visual similarity. That control produced an effect in the first block, a different pattern from semantic blocking.
